framework: AP United States History Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2026)
subject: United States History

source.licence: © College Board; structure + our own wording only

outcomes.text: Describe how native peoples migrated across North America and built increasingly complex societies by adapting to and reshaping their environments.
Explain how native societies adapted to and transformed their environments through farming, resource use and social organisation.
Explain how contact among Europeans, Native Americans and Africans produced the Columbian Exchange and major social, cultural and political change.
Explain how European expansion into the Americas sparked social, religious, political and economic rivalry within Europe.
Explain how the Columbian Exchange and the Spanish Empire changed population, economies and society.
Explain how Europeans and Native Americans clashed over religion, gender roles, family, land use and power.

topics.title: 1.2 Native American Societies Before European Contact

subtopics.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact

outcomes.text: Explain how maize spreading north from Mexico supported settlement, irrigation, economic growth and social variety in the Southwest.
Explain how dry Great Basin and Great Plains environments led societies to largely mobile lifestyles.
Explain how Northeast, Mississippi Valley and Atlantic coast societies mixed farming and hunting and favoured permanent villages.
Explain how Northwest and California societies lived by hunting, gathering and ocean resources and sometimes formed settled communities.
Explain how a hunt for wealth, economic and military rivalry and the wish to spread Christianity drove European exploration and conquest.

topics.title: 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest

subtopics.title: Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest

outcomes.text: Explain how American crops and mineral wealth boosted European population and helped move Europe from feudalism to capitalism.
Explain how better ships and organised trade such as joint-stock companies changed economies in Europe and the Americas.
Explain how epidemics and newly introduced crops and animals aided Spanish conquest and devastated native peoples.

topics.title: 1.5 Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System

subtopics.title: Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System

outcomes.text: Explain how the encomienda system used Native American labour for plantations and extracting precious metals.
Explain how Europeans partnered with some West African slaveholding groups to supply enslaved workers for Spanish plantations and mines.
Explain how the Spanish caste system defined the status of Europeans, Africans and Native Americans.

topics.title: 1.6 Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans

subtopics.title: Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans

outcomes.text: Explain how mutual misunderstanding marked early contact, while each group gradually borrowed useful elements from the other.
Explain how native peoples used diplomacy and warfare to defend sovereignty, prosperity, religion and gender relations against growing European demands.
Explain how contact sparked European debate over how to treat non-Europeans and growing justifications for subjugating Africans and Native Americans.
Explain how Europeans pursued different colonisation patterns shaped by imperial goals, cultures and environments, competing with each other and with American Indians.
Compare the economic and imperial aims of Spanish, French, Dutch and British colonisers and how they shaped colonies and relations with natives.
Explain how early 17th-century British Atlantic colonies developed regional differences due to environment, economy, culture and population.
Explain how competition for resources between Europeans and American Indians encouraged trade and caused conflict.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 2: British colonies

outcomes.text: Explain how British colonies' exchanges with Britain strengthened both ties to Britain and resistance to its control.
Explain how transatlantic commerce, religion, philosophy and politics shaped colonists' political and cultural attitudes.
Explain how English colonies built a slavery system reflecting their economic, demographic and geographic makeup.
Explain how Spanish efforts to extract wealth built institutions of subjugation, conversion and incorporation of natives and Africans.
Explain how few French and Dutch colonists relied on trade alliances and intermarriage with American Indians for furs.
Explain how many English migrants seeking opportunity farmed land taken from Native Americans and lived apart from them.
Explain how the Chesapeake and North Carolina grew rich on tobacco, first with indentured servants and later enslaved Africans.
Explain how Puritan New England built small towns, family farms and a mixed farming-and-commerce economy.
Explain how the middle colonies exported grain and attracted diverse, more tolerant societies.
Explain how southern coast and West Indies plantation economies relied on enslaved Africans who built their own cultures.
Explain how distance and light British oversight created unusually democratic self-government, from New England town meetings to southern planter rule.
Explain how an Atlantic economy exchanged goods and enslaved people among Europe, Africa and the Americas.
Explain how trade with Europeans changed American Indian communities and spread epidemic disease with major population shifts.
Explain how Britain tried mercantilist control over the colonies, though conflicts led to uneven enforcement.

topics.title: 2.5 Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

subtopics.title: Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

outcomes.text: Explain how European rivals and American Indians alternately accommodated and fought each other, forming and arming alliances.
Explain how British-Indian conflicts over land and boundaries led to wars such as Metacom's War.
Explain how resistance after the Pueblo Revolt led Spain to accept some American Indian cultural practices in the Southwest.
Explain how all British colonies joined the slave trade to different degrees, with most enslaved Africans going to the West Indies.
Explain how chattel slavery's growth brought racial laws banning interracial relations and making children of enslaved mothers enslaved for life.
Explain how Africans resisted openly and covertly and preserved family, gender systems, culture and religion.
Explain how religious and ethnic variety, the Great Awakening and Enlightenment ideas fostered pluralism and exchange.
Explain how colonies became gradually Anglicised, building English-style political communities with commercial ties, print culture and evangelicalism.
Explain how diverging interests of European leaders and colonists bred mistrust, with colonists protesting settlement, defence, self-rule and trade policy.
Explain how colonial resistance drew on local self-government, liberty ideas, Enlightenment thought, religious independence and distrust of imperial corruption.
Explain how British efforts to tighten control and colonists' pursuit of self-government led to independence and the Revolutionary War.
Explain how British, French and American Indian competition ended in the Seven Years' War with a British victory.
Explain how colonists' self-government ideals clashed with renewed imperial efforts, leading to independence and war.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 3: new nation

outcomes.text: Explain how revolutionary democratic and republican ideals inspired new forms of government.
Explain how revolutionary ideals reflected new 18th-century beliefs about politics, religion and society.
Explain how states and the nation wrote constitutions protecting liberties while limiting central power and excess popular influence.
Explain how new national culture and political institutions arose alongside persistent regional differences.
Explain how migration and competition over resources, borders and trade sharpened conflict among peoples and nations.
Explain how post-independence competition produced shifting alliances and cultural blending among groups.
Explain how continued European presence pushed the United States to safeguard borders, neutral trade and economic interests.

topics.title: 3.2 The Seven Years' War (The French and Indian War)

subtopics.title: The Seven Years' War (The French and Indian War)

outcomes.text: Explain how British-French rivalry grew as colonists expanded inland, threatening French-Indian trade and American Indian autonomy.
Explain how Britain's costly victory over France led to imperial efforts to raise revenue and tighten control.
Explain how limits on westward movement angered colonists, while native groups sought to keep trading and resist encroachment.
Explain how war-era struggles and new taxes without colonial representation began uniting colonists against constraints on economic and political rights.
Explain how colonial leaders justified resistance with British subjects' rights, individual rights, local self-rule and Enlightenment ideas.
Explain how leaders like Franklin and popular movements of workers, artisans and women energised the independence effort.
Explain how men and women mobilised financial and material support for the Patriot cause amid shortages and occupation.

topics.title: 3.4 Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution

subtopics.title: Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution

outcomes.text: Explain how Enlightenment ideas stressed individual talent over inherited privilege while religion strengthened belief in a people blessed with liberty.
Explain how belief in republican government and natural rights shaped Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence.
Explain how, despite loyalist opposition and British advantages, Patriot militias, the Continental Army, Washington, ideological commitment and European allies won.
Explain how awareness of inequality led some to call for abolition and wider political democracy.
Explain how women's wartime roles and Enlightenment ideas produced the ideal of republican motherhood.
Explain how the Revolution and Declaration of Independence inspired movements in France, Haiti and Latin America.
Explain how many state constitutions favoured legislatures and kept property qualifications for voting and citizenship.
Explain how the Articles created a weak central government whose trade, finance and unrest problems prompted calls for a stronger one.
Explain how the Northwest Ordinance admitted new states, promoted education and property protection and banned slavery in the territory.

topics.title: 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification

subtopics.title: The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification

outcomes.text: Explain how convention compromises covered slave states' representation and federal regulation of slavery, allowing the slave trade ban after 1808.
Explain how Federalists, backed by the Federalist Papers, overcame Anti-Federalists by promising a Bill of Rights.
Explain how convention delegates compromised to create a limited but dynamic central government with federalism and separated powers.
Explain how US diplomacy dealt with British and Spanish presence as settlers crossed the Appalachians and sought free Mississippi navigation.
Explain how the French Revolution's war with Britain strained US trade and foreign policy and deepened political disagreement.
Explain how an ambiguous federal-tribal relationship led to treaty problems and legal claims over seized land.
Explain how Spain expanded mission settlements in California using Indian labour, creating social mobility and cultural blending.
Explain how Washington and Adams created institutions and precedents that put the Constitution into practice.
Explain how 1790s disputes over state power, economic and foreign policy and liberty versus order produced Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties.
Explain how Washington's Farewell Address urged national unity and warned against factions and permanent foreign alliances.
Explain how national identity increasingly appeared in art, literature and architecture.
Explain how American Indian groups adjusted alliances to limit white settlement, and how British alliances heightened tensions with the US.
Explain how westward migration fed growing frontier cultures and social, political and ethnic tension.
Explain how slavery's expansion in the deep South and rising antislavery sentiment created distinct regional attitudes.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 4: democracy and culture

outcomes.text: Explain how the US developed a modern democracy and national culture while Americans sought to bring society closer to democratic ideals.
Explain how suffrage widened from property owners to all adult white men alongside the growth of parties.
Explain how a new national culture arose while various groups kept distinctive cultures.
Explain how new religious and intellectual movements led many Americans to pursue ideals outside government.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 4: economy and expansion

outcomes.text: Explain how new technology, agriculture and commerce transformed the economy, society and regional identities.
Explain how new transport systems and technologies sharply expanded manufacturing and farm production.
Explain how the market revolution changed society, workers' lives, gender and family relations.
Explain how economic development shaped settlement and trade, unifying the nation while fostering distinct regions.
Explain how interest in foreign trade and expansion shaped foreign policy and government and private initiatives.
Explain how the US sought territory across the continent and foreign trade to build an independent global presence.
Explain how western land acquisitions sparked conflict over extending slavery.

topics.title: 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson

subtopics.title: The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson

outcomes.text: Explain how early 1800s parties debated the tariff, federal powers and relations with European powers.
Explain how Supreme Court rulings established judicial primacy in interpreting the Constitution and federal law over state law.
Explain how, after the Louisiana Purchase, the US sought influence over North America through exploration, diplomacy and other means.
Explain how regional interests often outweighed national concerns in leaders' positions on slavery and the economy.
Explain how plans like the American System sparked debate over whether they favoured farming or industry and different sections.
Explain how compromises like the Missouri Compromise only briefly eased tension between slavery's opponents and defenders.
Explain how the US sought control in the Western Hemisphere through military action, Indian removal and the Monroe Doctrine.
Explain how entrepreneurs created a market revolution where producers and consumers connected through more organised manufacturing.
Name innovations such as textile machinery, steam engines, interchangeable parts, the telegraph and farm inventions that raised efficiency.
Explain how law and courts backed roads, canals and railroads that enlarged markets and linked regions.
Explain how Southern cotton and Northern manufacturing, banking and shipping built national and international commercial ties.
Explain how migrants filled industrial Northern cities and Americans moved west along the Ohio and Mississippi.
Explain how more workers, especially in factories, stopped living by semi-subsistence farming and produced goods for distant markets.
Explain how manufacturing raised prosperity for some, creating a middle class, a wealthy elite and a growing laboring poor.
Explain how family and gender roles shifted as domestic ideals separated public and private spheres.
Explain how Democrats under Jackson and Whigs under Clay arose, disagreeing on the national bank, tariffs and internal improvements.
Explain how frontier settlers pushed expansion, producing wars with American Indians and federal removal and relocation.

topics.title: 4.9 The Development of an American Culture

subtopics.title: The Development of an American Culture

outcomes.text: Explain how a national culture emerged blending American, European and regional elements.
Explain how liberal ideas from abroad and Romantic belief in human perfectibility shaped literature, art, philosophy and architecture.
Explain how democratic and individualist beliefs, reaction to rationalism and market-revolution change fed a Protestant Second Great Awakening.
Explain how voluntary organisations pursued temperance and other reforms to change behaviour and improve society.
Explain how abolitionism gradually won emancipation in the North and a larger free Black population even as states restricted Black rights.
Explain how antislavery movements grew in the North while Southern leaders defended slavery as a way of life.

subtopics.title: An age of reform: women's rights

outcomes.text: Explain how the women's rights movement sought equality, voiced at Seneca Falls, and later argued over narrowing goals to white women.

topics.title: 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic

subtopics.title: African Americans in the Early Republic

outcomes.text: Explain how enslaved and free Black Americans built communities and strategies to protect dignity and families and sought political change.

topics.title: 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic

subtopics.title: The Society of the South in the Early Republic

outcomes.text: Explain how Southern business leaders' reliance on staple exports fostered a distinct Southern identity.
Explain how soil depletion pushed slaveholders west to fertile land where slavery kept growing.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 5: expansion and migration

outcomes.text: Explain how the US grew more connected to the world, pursued expansion in the Western Hemisphere and drew many migrants.
Explain how popular enthusiasm for expansion, backed by economic and security interests, brought new territory, westward migration and overseas ventures.
Explain how Americans in the 1840s and 1850s kept debating rights and citizenship for various groups.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 5: sectional conflict and Civil War

outcomes.text: Explain how expansion and regional divisions turned debates over slavery and other issues into civil war.
Explain how ideological and economic differences over slavery produced diverging Northern and Southern responses.
Explain how slavery dominated 1850s politics, leading to the 1860 election and Southern secession.
Explain how the Union victory and contested Reconstruction settled slavery and secession but left federal power and citizenship rights unresolved.
Explain how Northern manpower and industry, Lincoln's leadership and emancipation brought Union victory.
Explain how the Civil War and Reconstruction ended slavery, changed state-federal relations and prompted debate over new rights definitions.
Explain how the wish for resources and opportunity or religious refuge drove migration and settlement in the West.
Explain how Manifest Destiny and belief in American superiority justified westward expansion but provoked competition and violence.
Explain how new legislation boosted western transportation and development during and after the Civil War.
Explain how interest in trade led to economic, diplomatic and cultural initiatives tying the US to Asia.
Explain how winning the Mexican-American War added huge western territory and raised questions about slavery, Indians and Mexicans there.
Explain how conflict with Mexican Americans and American Indians in newly taken regions undermined their economic self-sufficiency and cultures.
Explain how the Mexican Cession triggered fierce controversy over slavery in new territories.
Explain how courts and leaders tried to settle slavery in the territories through measures like the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act and Dred Scott, which ultimately failed.
Explain how many immigrants from Ireland and Germany settled in ethnic communities that preserved languages and customs.
Explain how a strongly anti-Catholic nativist movement sought to limit immigrants' political power and cultural influence.
Explain how the free-labour North and slave-labour South clashed, giving rise to the free-soil movement.
Explain how Black and white abolitionists campaigned visibly against slavery on moral grounds, helped escapes and sometimes accepted violence.
Explain how defenders of slavery relied on racial doctrines, claims that slavery was a social good, and constitutional and states' rights arguments.
Explain how slavery and nativism broke the Second Party System and produced sectional parties like the Northern Republicans.
Explain how Lincoln won in 1860 with no Southern electoral votes and most slave states then seceded, precipitating civil war.

topics.title: 5.8 Military Conflict in the Civil War

subtopics.title: Military Conflict in the Civil War

outcomes.text: Explain how both sides mobilised economies and societies for war while facing home-front opposition.
Explain how the Union won through better leadership and strategy, key victories, greater resources and destruction of Southern infrastructure.

topics.title: 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War

subtopics.title: Government Policies During the Civil War

outcomes.text: Explain how the Emancipation Proclamation reframed the war, blocked Confederate foreign support, and Black Americans helped by fleeing plantations and enlisting.
Explain how Lincoln used speeches like the Gettysburg Address to frame the fight against slavery as fulfilling founding ideals.
Explain how the 13th Amendment ended slavery and the 14th and 15th gave citizenship, equal protection and voting rights.
Explain how the women's rights movement was both energised and divided by the 14th and 15th Amendments.
Explain how Republican efforts to shift power to Congress and reorder race relations won short-term gains but ultimately failed.
Explain how planters kept most land and sharecropping limited freed people's self-sufficiency.
Explain how segregation, violence, court rulings and local tactics stripped African American rights, though the 14th and 15th Amendments later underpinned civil rights rulings.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 6: industrial capitalism

outcomes.text: Explain how technology, large-scale production and new markets drove the rise of industrial capitalism.
Explain how large-scale production, technology, communication networks and pro-growth policy produced rapid growth and business consolidation.
Explain how varied views on the economy and labour developed during panics and downturns.
Explain how new production and transport systems consolidated agriculture and spurred varied farmer responses.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 6: migration and the Gilded Age

outcomes.text: Explain how migration tied to industrialisation transformed urban and rural America socially and culturally.
Explain how international and internal migration grew cities and fostered an urban culture.
Explain how migrants went west for land and opportunity, often provoking competition and conflict.
Explain how the Gilded Age produced new movements, reform efforts and economic and social policy debates.
Explain how new cultural and intellectual movements both supported and challenged the Gilded Age social order.
Explain how social change prompted debate over citizenship, corruption and the proper relationship between business and government.
Explain how mechanisation raised farm output and lowered food prices.
Explain how farmers facing market consolidation and railroad dependence formed local and regional cooperatives.
Explain how post-Civil War subsidies for transport and communication opened new markets.
Explain how transcontinental railroads, mineral discoveries and policy promoted growth and created new communities.

topics.title: 6.3 Westward Expansion: Social and Cultural Development

subtopics.title: Westward Expansion: Social and Cultural Development

outcomes.text: Explain how migrants sought self-sufficiency and opportunity in the rural and boomtown West through railroads, mining, farming and ranching.
Explain how competition for land among settlers, American Indians and Mexican Americans, as the bison were wiped out, increased violent conflict.
Explain how the government broke treaties, answered resistance with force and confined American Indians to reservations.
Explain how many American Indians kept their cultures and identities despite assimilation policies and tried to build self-sustaining economies.
Explain how the "New South" industrialised partially but sharecropping and tenant farming stayed the main economic activity.
Explain how Plessy v. Ferguson upheld segregation and ended most Reconstruction gains while Black reformers kept fighting for equality.
Explain how technology, greater resource access, new finance and management structures, marketing and labour growth multiplied production.
Explain how business leaders consolidated corporations into trusts and holding companies, concentrating wealth.
Explain how businesses and policymakers looked abroad for influence over markets and resources in the Pacific Rim, Asia and Latin America.
Explain how falling prices raised real wages and living standards even as the gap between rich and poor widened.
Explain how labour and management fought over wages and conditions, with workers forming unions or confronting business leaders.
Explain how the industrial workforce grew, used more child labour and became more diverse through migration.

topics.title: 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

subtopics.title: Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

outcomes.text: Explain how growing cities drew immigrants from Asia and southern and eastern Europe and Black migrants fleeing poverty, persecution and limited mobility.
Explain how ethnic, racial and class neighbourhoods created new cultural opportunities.

topics.title: 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

subtopics.title: Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

outcomes.text: Explain how debates over assimilation and Americanisation accompanied migration as immigrants negotiated between old and new cultures.
Explain how Social Darwinism was used to justify the success of those at the top as appropriate and inevitable.
Explain how corporate demand for managers and clerical workers, education and leisure grew a distinct middle class and consumer culture.
Explain how the Gospel of Wealth held that the rich had a duty to help others, leading to philanthropy.
Explain how agrarians, utopians, socialists and Social Gospel advocates offered alternative visions for the economy and society.
Explain how women sought equality through settlement houses, voluntary groups, college and reform activism.

topics.title: 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age

subtopics.title: Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age

outcomes.text: Explain how some argued laissez-faire policies and competition spur growth and opposed intervention in downturns.
Explain how economic instability led farmers to form the Populist Party, seeking stronger government regulation.
Explain how major parties appealed to Civil War divisions and fought over tariffs and currency while reformers decried corruption.
Explain how urban political machines thrived by giving immigrants and the poor social services.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 7: growth and reform

outcomes.text: Explain how growth widened opportunity while economic instability led to new reform efforts.
Explain how the US kept shifting from a rural farm economy to an urban industrial economy led by big companies.
Explain how Progressives answered corruption, instability and social problems by calling for greater government action.
Explain how 1930s policymakers answered Depression unemployment by building a limited welfare state and redefining modern liberalism.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 7: culture, migration and world power

outcomes.text: Explain how communication and technology innovation grew mass culture while migration patterns shifted greatly.
Explain how popular culture gained influence amid debate over its effect on values, morals and national identity.
Explain how economic pressure, global events and politics sharply varied migrant numbers, origins and experiences.
Explain how a series of global conflicts made the US an international power and renewed debate over its world role.
Explain how new territorial ambitions in the Western Hemisphere and Pacific sparked debate over America's world role.
Explain how World War I and its aftermath intensified debate over national security and American interests.
Explain how World War II transformed American society and made the US a global political and military leader.
Explain how imperialists cited economics, racial theories, rivalry with Europe and the "closed" frontier to claim Americans should expand globally.
Explain how anti-imperialists cited self-determination, racial theories and isolationism to argue against overseas territory.
Explain how victory in the Spanish-American War brought Caribbean and Pacific islands, more involvement in Asia and suppression of Philippine nationalism.
Explain how muckraking journalists and largely middle- and upper-class reformers, many of them women, attacked corruption and injustice and worked for urban change.
Explain how national Progressives sought federal legislation to regulate the economy, expand democracy and promote moral reform, including Prohibition and women's suffrage amendments.
Explain how Progressives split on segregation, popular participation versus expert efficiency, and immigration restriction.

topics.title: 7.5 World War I: Military and Diplomacy

subtopics.title: World War I: Military and Diplomacy

outcomes.text: Explain how preservationists and conservationists both backed national parks but differed on responses to resource overuse.
Explain how the US entered World War I after neutrality, departing from non-involvement in European affairs, following Wilson's call to defend democratic principles.
Explain how US entry tipped the balance toward the Allies although American forces had a limited combat role.
Explain how the Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles or join the League of Nations despite Wilson's role.
Explain how wartime limits on speech and fear of radicalism fed a Red Scare and attacks on labour and immigrant culture.
Explain how European immigration peaked before World War I, then nativist quotas restricted southern and eastern European immigrants and added barriers for Asians.
Explain how war production demand and the Depression drew Americans to urban centres seeking opportunity.
Explain how the Great Migration moved African Americans fleeing segregation and violence to Northern and Western cities with new opportunity but continued discrimination.
Explain how new technology and manufacturing focused the economy on consumer goods, raising living standards, mobility and communications.
Explain how mass media like radio and cinema spread national culture and awareness of regional cultures.
Explain how by 1920 most Americans lived in cities, which offered new opportunities to women and migrants.
Explain how migration produced new art and literature expressing ethnic and regional identities, such as the Harlem Renaissance.
Explain how 1920s controversies arose over gender roles, modernism, science, religion, race and immigration.
Explain how credit and market instability, especially the Great Depression, led to calls for stronger financial regulation.
Explain how Roosevelt's New Deal used government power for relief, recovery and economic reform.
Explain how radical, union and populist movements pushed Roosevelt further, while conservatives in Congress and the Court tried to limit the New Deal.
Explain how the New Deal left reforms, regulatory agencies and a political realignment toward the Democratic Party, though it did not end the Depression.
Explain how after World War I the US pursued unilateral policy using investment, treaties and limited intervention while staying isolationist.
Explain how most Americans opposed military action against Nazi Germany and Japan in the 1930s until Pearl Harbor.
Explain how mass mobilization ended the Depression and US industry supplied allies and millions of troops.
Explain how war mobilization and service gave women and minorities temporary economic gains and sparked debate over segregation, while internment of Japanese Americans challenged civil liberties.
Explain how migration from Mexico and the hemisphere grew despite contradictory government policies.
Explain how Americans saw the war as a fight for freedom and democracy against fascism, reinforced by revelations of Japanese atrocities, concentration camps and the Holocaust.
Explain how Allied cooperation, technology, service members and campaigns like island-hopping and D-Day won the war, while atomic bombs hastened the end and sparked moral debate.
Explain how a ruined Asia and Europe and the dominant US role in victory and peace left the US as the world's most powerful nation.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 8: Cold War leadership

outcomes.text: Explain how the US met an unstable postwar world by asserting global leadership with major domestic and international consequences.
Explain how the US waged a cold war against the Soviet Union to limit Communism, build a free-market global economy and create international security.
Explain how Cold War policies caused debate over federal power and acceptable means while protecting civil liberties.

subtopics.title: Key concepts of Period 8: rights and society

outcomes.text: Explain how new civil rights movements and liberal efforts to expand government produced varied political and cultural responses.
Explain how activists achieved some legal and political successes ending segregation, though progress toward equality was slow.
Explain how identity, social justice and environmental movements emerged from social conditions and the civil rights movement.
Explain how liberalism shaped postwar politics and courts but faced attacks from both the left and a resurgent conservative movement.
Explain how postwar economic and demographic change had far-reaching effects on society, politics and culture.
Explain how rapid economic and social change fostered postwar optimism.
Explain how new demographic and social developments and Cold War anxiety changed culture and sparked divisive debates.
Explain how the wartime alliance dissolved and the US built a policy of collective security, aid and economic institutions to bolster non-Communist nations.
Explain how the US sought to contain communism through measures including major wars in Korea and Vietnam.
Explain how the Cold War alternated between direct and indirect military confrontation and periods of coexistence (detente).
Explain how Americans debated policies to expose suspected communists at home even as both parties backed containment.
Explain how private sector growth, federal spending, the baby boom and technology drove economic growth.
Explain how expanded higher education and technology raised mobility, sending the middle class to suburbs and many to the South and West as the Sun Belt rose.
Explain how increasingly uniform postwar mass culture prompted challenges to conformity by artists, intellectuals and rebellious youth.

topics.title: 8.6 Early Steps in the Civil Rights Movement (1940s and 1950s)

subtopics.title: Early Steps in the Civil Rights Movement (1940s and 1950s)

outcomes.text: Explain how all three federal branches promoted racial equality through measures such as armed forces desegregation, Brown v. Board of Education and the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Explain how decolonisation and new nationalist movements led both Cold War sides to court non-aligned nations in Africa, the Middle East and Asia.
Explain how Cold War rivalry extended to Latin America, where the US backed non-Communist regimes of varying democratic commitment.
Explain how Americans debated a large nuclear arsenal, the military-industrial complex and executive power in foreign and military policy.
Explain how advocates raised concerns about persistent poverty despite overall postwar affluence.
Explain how liberalism, based on anti-communism abroad and faith in government at home, reached its peak by the mid-1960s.
Explain how Johnson's Great Society used federal programs to end discrimination and poverty, and Supreme Court rulings expanded civil rights and liberties.
Explain how immigrants from around the world sought opportunity, especially after the 1965 immigration laws.

topics.title: 8.10 The African American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)

subtopics.title: The African American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)

outcomes.text: Explain how civil rights leaders like Martin Luther King Jr. fought discrimination through legal challenges, direct action and nonviolent protest.
Explain how continuing resistance slowed desegregation, causing unrest and debate among activists over nonviolence after 1965.
Explain how feminist and LGBTQ+ activists mobilised for legal, economic and social equality.
Explain how Latino, American Indian and Asian American movements demanded equality and redress of past injustices.
Explain how the 1960s counterculture, including feminists and young people, rejected parents' values, added informality and urged changes in sexual norms.
Explain how the Vietnam War sparked large anti-war protests, sometimes violent, ending broad consensus on anti-communist foreign policy.
Explain how some on the left rejected liberal policies as doing too little on racial and economic inequality and pursuing immoral policies abroad.

topics.title: 8.13 The Environment and Natural Resources from 1968 to 1980

subtopics.title: The Environment and Natural Resources from 1968 to 1980

outcomes.text: Explain how ideology, military and economic concerns shaped Middle East involvement, and oil crises led to attempts at a national energy policy.
Explain how environmental problems and accidents grew the environmental movement and led to new federal programs and regulations.
Explain how 1960s conservatives challenged liberal laws and perceived moral decline, seeking a smaller federal role and a tougher foreign policy.
Explain how public trust in government's ability to solve problems fell in the 1970s amid economic trouble, scandal and foreign policy crises.
Explain how the 1970s saw sharper conservative-liberal clashes over social issues, federal power, race and individual rights.
Explain how evangelical churches grew rapidly with greater political activism by religious conservatives.
Explain how an ascendant conservative movement reached political and policy goals in the 1980s and kept shaping public debate.
Explain how conservative beliefs in traditional values and reduced government advanced in politics after 1980.
Explain how the nation underwent major technological, economic and demographic change into the 21st century.
Explain how new science and technology boosted the economy and transformed society while manufacturing declined.
Explain how demographic shifts had significant cultural and political consequences.
Explain how the end of the Cold War and new challenges forced the US to redefine foreign policy and its world role.
Explain how Reagan's interventionist foreign policy continued under later administrations after the Cold War.
Explain how after September 11, 2001 foreign policy focused on fighting terrorism worldwide.
Explain how Reagan's 1980 victory let conservatives enact tax cuts and continue deregulation.
Explain how conservatives called liberal programs counterproductive, yet efforts to shrink government met inertia and opposition as many programs stayed popular.
Explain how policy debates continued over free-trade agreements, the social safety net and financial system reform.
Explain how intense debates continued over immigration, diversity, gender roles and family structures.

topics.title: 9.3 The End of the Cold War

subtopics.title: The End of the Cold War

outcomes.text: Explain how Reagan opposed communism through speeches, diplomacy, limited interventions and a nuclear and conventional weapons buildup.

Explain how the Cold War's end brought new diplomatic ties, new interventions and peacekeeping, and debate over the use of American power.
Explain how digital communications raised productivity and worldwide economic participation.
Explain how computing, mobile technology and the internet transformed daily life, information access and social networks.
Explain how service jobs grew while manufacturing jobs and union membership fell.
